title: Closing Our Leadership Rings
author: Nick Hart
summary: Nick Hart uses the metaphor of 'closing the rings' between a leadership team's imagined picture of an organization and its actual reality to argue that no individual leader, however senior, can fully know the truth of daily life on the ground. He proposes a specific linguistic habit -- replacing 'Any questions?' with 'What have I missed?' -- as a low-cost way to signal genuinely that a leader expects to have gotten something wrong, which in turn opens genuine disclosure rather than performative silence. Hart extends the argument by warning that asking only a narrow, similarly-positioned circle 'What have we missed?' will not close the gap; leadership teams must deliberately widen who they ask, including people whose backgrounds and vantage points differ from their own. The second half of the piece develops a sense-making/sense-giving framework: understanding reality collectively (sense making) is necessary but not sufficient, because leaders must also actively help others interpret that reality (sense giving) through framing change, holding ambiguity honestly, stabilizing meaning during disruption, amplifying other voices, and closing the feedback loop. Throughout, Hart frames this as fundamentally relational rather than command-and-control leadership.
points: Hart's central metaphor -- closing the gap ('rings') between a leadership team's imagined reality and the organization's actual reality -- reframes leadership accuracy as a collective, not individual, achievement.

The reframe from 'Any questions?' to 'What have I missed?' is offered as a concrete, low-cost habit that signals genuine openness to being wrong rather than a performative gesture toward collegiality.

Hart warns that widening the circle of who leaders ask matters as much as asking at all -- a leadership team with a narrow, similar background will structurally fail to close its rings even if it asks the question often.

The sense making / sense giving distinction argues that understanding reality is necessary but insufficient: leaders must also actively help others interpret that reality, or leadership 'becomes an internal exercise only.'

Hart's five sense-giving examples (framing change, holding ambiguity, stabilising meaning, amplifying voices, closing the loop) each swap a command-and-control script for a relational one, offering leaders literal alternative phrasing.
quotes: No individual leader can possibly know the full reality of school life. And the more senior that leader is, the less likely it is that they can know the reality because truth doesn't rise to the top.
It is a fundamental job of a school leader to aim to close their rings between the reality of school life and what we imagine it to be.
Too often, people ask 'Any questions?'. While seemingly harmless, this phrase and how it is delivered is loaded with meaning.
If a leadership team all have a similar background and similar experiences, there is a very real risk that they are hampered from the outset in closing their leadership rings.
Making sense without giving sense risks leadership becoming an internal exercise only. Closing the rings requires us not just to understand reality, but to help others navigate it with us.

This is a relational act, not a command and control one. The goal is not to impose a fixed narrative or tell others what to think, but to stabilise meaning in times of disruption, to frame change without forcing it, and to provide clarity without the false promise of certainty.
Colleagues often look to leaders for certainty, especially during times of disruption. But offering false certainty can backfire.

After gathering feedback, sense giving closes the leadership rings by returning to the community with Here's what you told us, here's how we've interpreted it, and here's how it has shaped our decisions.
